newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Paramilitary boss stands in Bosnia election.
newsitem.headline: Paramilitary boss stands in Bosnia election.

text.p: Ljubisa Savic displays a remarkable talent for adapting to his times. As the commander of Serb paramilitary troops during the Bosnian war, he led ethnic cleansing operations in his home town of Bijeljina.
Now the guns are silent, he is running as a candidate in Bosnia's first post-war elections on September 14.
Known by his nom de guerre, "Major Mauser," the leader of the "Panthers" corps describes himself as a pragmatist and reluctant ethnic cleanser who had the best interests of the Moslems at heart.
A grim, stocky man, Savic held the fate of many Moslem families in his hands during the war.

He says expulsions were inevitable once the war started. "If municipal or military authorities took advantage of the situation to rob them as they were being transported, at least they arrived safely," said Savic, who has traded his camouflage fatigues for black trousers and a black leather jacket.
Human rights workers and refugees painted a different picture. They describe terrifying scenes with Moslem families robbed and brutally driven out of their flats.
Moslem refugees freeze at the mere mention of Mauser's name. They fear that if they talk about their experience they will ruin any chance of moving back.
Western governments did not have Savic in mind when they hailed the Bosnian elections as an opportunity to reunify the divided country and promote moderate alternatives to nationalist parties.

Because he has not been indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for former Yugoslavia, Savic can stand for office and his opposition party qualifies for campaign funds paid for by Western powers.

On April 1, 1992, a full month before Sarajevo came under shell fire, Serb paramilitaries backed by the Yugoslav army swept through the towns of Bijeljina and Zvornik to carve out a strategic corridor in eastern Bosnia.

Local Moslem leaders were rounded up in Bijeljina and executed. Mercenaries led by Savic and the notorious Zeljko Raznatovic "Arkan" purged tens of thousands of Moslems from Bijeljina and blew up a mosque in the town centre.

Opponents say Savic and Arkan were hired to do Serbia's bidding in Bosnia. Savic insists he is just an ordinary man, an unemployed social worker, who was chosen by his neighbours to defend Serb homes. "Somebody has to do it, somebody had to have the guts."

Straddling an important crossroads connecting Bosnian Serb territory to neighbourning Serbia. Bijeljina propspered from wartime looting and smuggling. While Serb soldiers on the front line survived on meagre rations, war profiteers gambled until dawn at Bijeljina's thriving casinos.
The property and hard currency stolen from Moslem families enriched many in Bijeljina but Savic insists he never profited from the war.

Savic no longer issues calls to arms. Now he speaks about the need for economic reconstruction and castigates the "thieves and murderers" in Radovan Karadzic's Serb Democratic Party (SDS), which runs Bosnia's Serb republic.

Among Serbs, Savic is a local hero who "liberated' Bijeljina. They have a chance to vote for him on September 14 as a candidate for the Bosnian Serb assembly for the Democratic Patriotic Bloc, an opposition party led by the mayor of Banja Luka.

Savic reserves his most bitter words for his own leaders in Pale, outside Sarajevo, who he expects to win a majority. The disagreement is not over ideology -- as nearly all the Serb parties want nothing to do with a multi-ethnic, unified Bosnia -- but over means.
He says he wants Bijeljina back in the hands of "honest" local people instead of the SDS, which keeps tight control of the town's economy.
Although he dismisses the elections as a "circus" he says he is standing as a candidate so he can tell his children that, "I tried to change something".

For Savic, the "cleansing" apparently did not go far enough. "The Islamic religion is aggressive and they want to spread it. They need an embryo of an Islamic state in Europe. They will keep fighting for it over many years ... They are already taking over France and they're moving into London.".
